question: Given the nine-sided regular polygon \(A_1 A_2 A_3 A_4 A_5 A_6 A_7 A_8 A_9,\) how many distinct equilateral triangles in the plane of the polygon have at least two vertices in the set \(\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_9\}?\)
solution:
Any two distinct points determine exactly two equilateral triangles, one on each side of the line joining them. There are \(\binom{9}{2}=36\) pairs of polygon vertices, so choosing a pair and an equilateral completion gives
\[
2\binom{9}{2}=72
\]
counts. Every triangle requested in the question appears in this count because it contains at least one such pair.

A triangle with exactly two polygon vertices is counted once. A triangle with three polygon vertices is counted three times, once for each side. We therefore need to identify the latter triangles.

Consecutive vertices of the regular nonagon are \(360^\circ/9=40^\circ\) apart about its center. An equilateral triangle on the same circumcircle has three \(60^\circ\) inscribed angles, so each arc between consecutive triangle vertices measures \(120^\circ\). Its vertices must therefore occur every three polygon vertices. The only such triangles are
\[
A_1A_4A_7,\qquad A_2A_5A_8,\qquad A_3A_6A_9.
\]
Each was counted three times and should remain once, so we remove two counts for each. The number of distinct triangles is
\[
72-2\cdot3=\boxed{66},
\]
which is choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

edges.reason: These relations provide circle-angle context. The half-central-angle theorem for one intercepted arc can be proved with radii and triangle angles without the separate equal-chord equivalences.
edges.scope: Relating central angles, chords and arcs before the inscribed-angle theorem

edges.reason: Interior angle sums help with angle work. However, radius and apothem come from the central angle 360/n and a right triangle, and the interior angle follows from the central angle too.
The triangle circumcircle introduces circles through all vertices, which eases the generalization. Regular polygon center and radius can be defined via symmetry or equal division of a circle.
edges.scope: circumscribed circle of a regular polygon

edges.reason: The criterion distinguishes combinations from permutations, requiring the ordered-selection concept for that contrast even though unordered selection can be introduced independently.

Dividing ordered counts by internal permutations supplies a standard derivation. Evaluating the supplied factorial quotient or a Pascal recurrence does not require first computing a permutation number.
C(n,k) evaluates an unordered selection count; the combination concept gives the object and its non-order-sensitive meaning.
Uniform contributions are often totaled by multiplication, which helps. Double counting itself only needs two summations of one set, and either summation can be done by direct addition.
edges.scope: product counts of uniform incidence contributions
